t: Minimum Operations to Reach Target Array
o: Each operation picks a value x and rewrites every maximal block of x's to their target values. We must make nums equal to target with fewest operations. In example 1 the mismatches hold values 1 and 2, and two operations (x=1, then x=2) suffice. In example 2 only value 4 is mismatched, so one operation on x=4 fixes both ends at once. In example 3 the mismatched values are 7 and 9, giving 2. Constraints allow O(n log n), so we just need the right counting observation.
k: A position's value only ever changes when it is fixed (set to its target), so the operation that fixes position i must use x equal to the ORIGINAL nums[i].
Therefore every distinct value v that appears at a mismatched position forces at least one operation with x=v, and performing one operation per such value suffices.

a.i: Scan both arrays; collect the set of nums[i] values wherever nums[i] != target[i]. The answer is the size of that set. Lower bound: a mismatched cell can only be overwritten by an operation whose x equals its current value, and its current value never changes until it is fixed, so each distinct mismatched value needs its own operation. Upper bound: issuing one operation per distinct value fixes all cells of that value and disturbs nothing else.
s: Build a set of nums[i] for all i with nums[i] != target[i].
a.sp: O(n) — the set of mismatched values

w: The whole problem collapses to one observation: cells only change when they are fixed, so the fixing operation's x must equal the cell's original value. Pitfall: do not simulate the operations; just count distinct mismatched values. Edge cases: identical arrays give 0; a single value spanning many mismatched cells costs only 1. Follow-up: what if the operation rewrote only one segment instead of all? Then a stack/interval-decomposition analysis would be needed.
